title: Ashbacker Radio Corp. v. Federal Communications Commission
lead: Two radio applications cannot coexist on the requested frequency, but the agency grants one before scheduling the other’s hearing.

actors.name: Ashbacker Radio Corporation
actors.role: Operator of Muskegon station WKBZ seeking a frequency change.

actors.name: Fetzer Broadcasting
actors.role: Applicant for a new Grand Rapids station on the same frequency.

actors.name: Federal Communications Commission (FCC)
actors.role: Agency granting Fetzer’s permit and defending Ashbacker’s later hearing opportunity.

proceedings: The FCC granted Fetzer without a hearing and set Ashbacker for a later hearing, then denied relief against Fetzer’s grant.
The D.C. Court of Appeals dismissed Ashbacker’s appeal without opinion.
The Supreme Court reversed that dismissal because the sequence impaired the statutory hearing right.
limits: The 1945 decision applied then-§ 309(a), not the later § 309(e) structure. No completed Ashbacker merits hearing or final licensing denial preceded review, and the Court selected no winning broadcaster.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Two bona fide applications compete for one usable frequency
sections.cue: Why was this more than ordinary economic competition?
paragraphs: In March 1944 Fetzer Broadcasting sought a Grand Rapids station on 1230 kilocycles, 250 watts, and unlimited time. Before decision, Ashbacker applied in May to move its existing Muskegon WKBZ station from 1490 to 1230 with the same power and hours.

The Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, found simultaneous operation would cause intolerable interference. The applications were actually mutually exclusive; the record suggested no feasible adjustment allowing both, disqualifying deadline, or bad-faith filing by Ashbacker.

sections.title: The Commission gives Fetzer a permit and Ashbacker a later hearing
sections.cue: How did the grant alter the hearing’s stakes?
paragraphs: In June the FCC granted Fetzer without hearing and on the same day designated Ashbacker for a hearing. Ashbacker requested hearing, rehearing, and relief against that grant. The Commission refused, saying it had not denied Ashbacker’s application and could still choose the better public-interest proposal later.

Yet the hearing notice made Ashbacker establish, among other things, the extent of interference with the already-authorized station and resolve specified issues favorably on a formal record. The matter reaching court was that designation and burden, not a completed comparative hearing followed by denial.

Ashbacker appealed the Fetzer construction permit under § 402(b)(2) as an adversely affected person. The D.C. Court of Appeals dismissed on the FCC’s jurisdictional motion without opinion, and the Supreme Court granted review.

sources.pinpoint: Agency action; Judicial proceedings; 326 U.S. at 328–331,334

sections.title: Douglas reads the summary-grant power with the hearing entitlement
sections.cue: Why did a formally available hearing become inadequate?
paragraphs: Then-§ 309(a) allowed grants on examination when public interest, convenience, or necessity supported approval; otherwise it required notice and opportunity for hearing. Douglas’s majority read both commands together. Granting one mutually exclusive application could not render the other’s hearing empty merely because summary-grant power existed in isolation.

The interference finding made the imposed showing impossible on the given terms. Ashbacker effectively had to obtain rehearing of a competitor’s grant instead of ordinary consideration of its own application. FCC regulations encouraging coordinated scheduling and consolidation of conflicting matters reinforced the conclusion without prescribing every procedural detail.

No licensee acquired a vested frequency property right, but modification, suspension, and revocation themselves required procedures protecting the incumbent. Fetzer’s authorization thus turned Ashbacker into a newcomer seeking displacement. The grant was not genuinely provisional, a stay had been denied, and the agency identified no urgent public need to act first. Urgency could not be inferred simply from the decision to grant.

sections.title: The hearing injury supports appeal before construction is complete
sections.cue: Could the operating-license stage cure the omission?
paragraphs: Precedent allowed appeals by economically injured competitors and licensees affected by interfering grants. Ashbacker was at least as adversely affected because its hearing remained only in form. That injury supported the appeal dismissed below.

The construction permit differed from the operating license issued after compliance under § 319(b). Later refusal ordinarily required a newly known or arising public-interest problem, and the parties conceded Ashbacker could not use that later stage to attack the original failure to hear its application. It did not have to wait until construction made the deprivation harder to remedy.

sources.pinpoint: Appeal and operating license; 326 U.S. at 333–334 & n.10

sections.title: Frankfurter would repair the hearing while permitting a qualified initial grant
sections.cue: Where did the disagreement over agency flexibility lie?
paragraphs: Frankfurter, joined by Rutledge, also regarded the interference condition as defective. He nevertheless emphasized specialized public-interest administration and Congress’s express allowance for grants on examination. He assumed both applications had been examined and thought the agency could grant Fetzer conditionally, then modify the authorization if Ashbacker proved superior. His notes described earlier conflicting-application practice and modification powers.

He would return the matter to revise the hearing order so Ashbacker could make its comparative case, while preserving the qualified grant. The dissent therefore did not approve a useless hearing; it disputed the majority’s limit on sequencing.

The Supreme Court reversed the appellate dismissal, five to two among participating Justices. Black and Jackson took no part. Its rationale required a meaningful opportunity for both bona fide, mutually exclusive applicants before a grant practically defeated one. It did not award a license, decide broadcaster superiority, or supply rules for later auctions and coexistence scenarios discussed editorially.

sources.pinpoint: Dissent; Judgment; 326 U.S. at 334–339 & dissent nn.1–3
